draft.title: Sketching derivative and antiderivative graphs
card: The derivative graph shows the gradient of the original graph. Where the original rises, the derivative is above the x-axis. Where it falls, the derivative is below.
Where the original has a turning point, the derivative graph crosses the x-axis, because the gradient is zero.
Going the other way, an antiderivative has the given graph as its gradient. Where the given graph is positive, the antiderivative rises. Where it is negative, it falls.
Example: a parabola that opens upward has a derivative that is a straight line with positive gradient, crossing the x-axis at the parabola's lowest point.
draft.remember: The original's gradient is the derivative's height.

a.q: A graph rises, reaches a peak, then falls. What does its derivative graph do around the peak?
opts: Goes from above the x-axis to below it
Goes from below the x-axis to above it
Stays above the x-axis the whole time
Has a peak at the same x-value
a.why: Before the peak the gradient is positive, at the peak it is zero, and after it the gradient is negative. So the derivative crosses the x-axis from above to below. A peak in the original does not give a peak in the derivative.
a.clue: Think about the sign of the gradient before and after the peak.

b.q: A graph y = f(x) is below the x-axis for x < 2 and above it for x > 2. What is true of an antiderivative of f?
opts: It falls until x = 2, then rises
It rises until x = 2, then falls
It is below the x-axis for x < 2
It is above the x-axis for x > 2
b.why: The antiderivative has gradient f(x). Where f is negative it falls, and where f is positive it rises, so it has a lowest point at x = 2. Its own height is not set by the sign of f, so the last two options mix up height and gradient.
b.clue: The sign of f gives the gradient of the antiderivative, not its height.

a.best: Goes from above the x-axis to below it

b.best: It falls until x = 2, then rises

problems.detail: Why (b) says 'the last two options mix up height and gradient', but the options are shuffled. In the order shown, the height options are the second and third, and the last option is the correct one. The why should name the height options by their content, not their position.

final.title: Sketching derivative and antiderivative graphs
card: The derivative graph shows the gradient of the original graph. Where the original rises, the derivative is above the x-axis. Where it falls, the derivative is below.
Where the original has a turning point, the derivative graph crosses the x-axis, because the gradient is zero.
Going the other way, an antiderivative has the given graph as its gradient. Where the given graph is positive, the antiderivative rises. Where it is negative, it falls.
Example: a parabola that is concave up has a derivative that is a straight line with positive gradient, crossing the x-axis at the parabola's turning point.

4.alt: A concave up parabola \(y = f(x) = (x - 1)^{2} - 2\) and its derivative \(y = f'(x) = 2(x - 1)\), a straight line with positive gradient. The line crosses the x-axis at \(x = 1\), the x-value of the parabola's turning point.

final.remember: The original's gradient is the derivative's height.

a.q: A graph rises to a local maximum, then falls. What does its derivative graph do around the local maximum?
opts: Goes from above the x-axis to below it
Goes from below the x-axis to above it
Stays above the x-axis the whole time
Has a local maximum at the same x-value
a.why: Before the local maximum the gradient is positive, at the local maximum it is zero, and after it the gradient is negative. So the derivative crosses the x-axis from above to below. A local maximum in the original does not give a local maximum in the derivative.
a.clue: Think about the sign of the gradient before and after the local maximum.

b.q: A graph \(y = f(x)\) is below the x-axis for \(x < 2\) and above it for \(x > 2\). What is true of an antiderivative of \(f\)?
opts: It falls until \(x = 2\), then rises
It rises until \(x = 2\), then falls
It is below the x-axis for \(x < 2\)
It is above the x-axis for \(x > 2\)
b.why: The antiderivative has gradient \(f(x)\). Where \(f\) is negative it falls, and where \(f\) is positive it rises, so it has a local minimum at \(x = 2\). The options saying it is below the x-axis for \(x < 2\) or above it for \(x > 2\) mix up height and gradient: the sign of \(f\) sets the antiderivative's gradient, not its height.
b.clue: The sign of \(f\) gives the gradient of the antiderivative, not its height.
